name: Savosavo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wegener, Claudia U. 2008. A grammar of Savosavo, a Papuan language of the Solomon Islands. PhD thesis, Radboud Universiteit Nijmegen (MPI Series in Psycholinguistics 51). Open at MPG PuRe.
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.3 Stress and 2.3.1 Root stress, pp. 24-25; Table 2.6 p. 25; sec. 2.3.2 Influence of affixes and clitics on stress, pp. 26-28, Table 2.7 p. 28.
catalog_quote: Stress assignment proceeds from the end of the root. Therefore, if there is more than one stressed syllable in a root, the rightmost stressed syllable is analyzed as carrying primary stress. ... The general rule for stress in roots in a one- or two-word sentence where the bare root is used is that the penultimate syllable of a root carries primary stress (marked by ˈ in the examples). Furthermore, whenever primary stress is on a non-initial syllable, the initial syllable receives secondary stress (indicated by ˌ in the examples), i.e. it is (almost) as prominent as the primarily stressed syllable. Disyllabic roots are without exception stressed on the first syllable, e.g. ˈtuvi 'house'. Trisyllabic roots are either stressed on the first or the second syllable, and therefore partly deviate from the general pattern described above. It is not predictable which trisyllabic roots are stressed on the first syllable and which on the second. From a sample of 292, about 75% are stressed on the penultimate syllable (and also have secondary stress on the first). The remaining 25% are stressed on the first syllable. ... Four-syllable roots are stressed on the penultimate syllable, the first syllable carries secondary stress (e.g. ˌkenaˈghuli 'fishing hook'). ... Both V and CV syllables can take primary or secondary stress. ... As the examples show, syllable structure does not have an influence on stress assignment.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default: primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the root, counted from the right edge; disyllabic roots always initial(=penult), four-syllable roots penult; but about a quarter of trisyllabic roots are lexically stressed on the initial (antepenultimate) syllable instead, with no phonological conditioning. Syllable structure (V vs CV) plays no role. Stressed syllables are longer, more intense, sometimes higher-pitched (auditory impression plus qualitative PRAAT analysis).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Whenever primary stress is non-initial, the initial syllable carries secondary stress, described as (almost) as prominent as the primary; in roots with more than one stressed syllable the rightmost is analysed as primary. Roots of 5+ syllables are historically complex and combine the patterns of their parts.
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllabic roots: ~25% of 292 stressed on first syllable (e.g. ˈadaki 'woman', ˈsivugha 'hair') vs 75% penult (aˈgutu 'work'); unpredictable. Suffixes/enclitics alter stress lexically: adding monosyllabic -ghu 'NMLZ' or =gha 'PL' to disyllabic roots leaves stress on the first syllable in 68% of 592 roots but moves it to the second in 32% (ˈsotaghu vs eˈpighu), 'has to be learned along with the root'; initial-stressed trisyllables shift to penult when suffixed (ˈadaki -> adaˈkigha); 9% of 213 four-syllable roots (all nouns) shift from 3rd to 4th syllable; object suffixes normally do not shift stress; one-consonant prefixes never affect stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Rule stated for bare roots in one- or two-word utterances (citation-like forms); clitics form a phonological word with the host; sec. 2.3.2 covers affix/clitic effects; author notes further investigation needed for combined suffixes/enclitics. Language-level description of Savosavo (Savo Island), no dialect restriction stated.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Savosavo (svs, savo1255) of Savo Island as a whole; no dialect restriction. The 2012 Mouton grammar is the published revision of the same work.

tone.quote: Savosavo has been analysed as a stress language based primarily on auditory impression, with additional qualitative analyses in [1]. Generally, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a root; initial syllables receive a secondary stress if primary stress is on a non-initial syllable. Impressionistically, stressed syllables have been associated with longer duration, clearer pronunciation, higher intensity and sometimes higher pitch. [...] The Savosavo data demonstrates a consistency in acoustic correlates sufficient to corroborate its status as a lexical stress language. Its lexical prosody mirrors that of English, a well-studied stress language.
